🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

About five hundred years ago, the most famous teacher in Europe was a Dutchman named Erasmus. One summer, while staying with his friend Thomas More in London, he wrote a funny little book. In it, a character named Folly (which means foolishness) stands up in front of a crowd and gives a speech praising... herself!

Folly says everyone needs her. Friends get along because they overlook each other's silly habits. Parents think their children are the most wonderful in the world. People laugh, play and fall in love, and all of that, she says, is a little bit foolish. Then she teases all sorts of grown-ups who think they are very wise.

blocks.name: gb-folly
blocks.cap: Folly in the middle, and the kinds of people she teases. Tap a group.

blocks.html: The trick of the book is that we never quite know when to believe Folly. Sometimes she is just being silly. Sometimes she says something true that a serious person would not dare to say.

🧩 Try this: a mock speech

A speech in praise of something silly. Pick something small and silly (a sock with a hole, a squeaky door, a puddle) and write five sentences praising it as if it were the most important thing in the world. Read it aloud in a grand voice. Did any of your jokes turn out to be a little bit true?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Desiderius Erasmus (c. 1466–1536) was born in Rotterdam, trained as a priest, and became the leading humanist of northern Europe: a scholar who went back to the Greek and Latin classics, and to the earliest texts of the Bible, to renew learning and Christian life. He wrote in Latin, the shared language of educated Europe, and his books sold everywhere the new printing presses reached.

In 1509, riding back from Italy to England, he thought up a speech for Folly. He wrote it at Thomas More's house and dedicated it to More; the Latin title, Moriae Encomium, means "The Praise of Folly" and also puns on More's name. It was printed in 1511 and became one of the best sellers of the century.

head: Part
What Folly does
The tone
rows: Introduces her family and companions and claims credit for youth, love, friendship and fun
Parades the foolish: hunters, gamblers, scholars, poets, philosophers, theologians, monks, rulers, popes
Says Christian faith itself looks like folly to the world, and that the greatest joy is a kind of holy madness
blocks.cap: The shape of the speech (our outline).

blocks.html: The middle part is the sharpest. Erasmus lets Folly mock scholars who argue over tiny questions, monks who care more for rules than for kindness, and church leaders who live like princes. He was a Catholic priest who wanted the church reformed from within, and these pages were read all over Europe.

Irony is the key to the book. The speaker is Folly, so we cannot simply believe her or simply dismiss her. Some of her praise is silly; some is a wise truth in a fool's costume. Readers have to decide, sentence by sentence, which is which.

In 1516 Erasmus published a printed edition of the Greek New Testament with a fresh Latin translation, a landmark of scholarship. A year later Martin Luther began the Protestant Reformation. People said "Erasmus laid the egg that Luther hatched," because both criticized abuses in the church. But Erasmus stayed Catholic and disagreed with Luther in print, especially about free will. Many Protestants thought him too timid, and many Catholics thought him too critical, a position he accepted as the price of moderation.
Thinking satire means hatred. Erasmus teases the people he knew best: scholars like himself, churchmen like himself. Satire can come from love of what a thing ought to be.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Folly belongs to a long line of wise fools: the jesters of royal courts, Shakespeare's Feste and Lear's Fool, and Cervantes's Sancho Panza, all later on this ladder. Behind them is St. Paul's line that God chose "the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1 Corinthians 1:27), which Folly quotes near the end.

items: Is a little foolishness necessary for friendship and family life? Where is the line between kindness and pretending?
Can you criticize an institution you love? What is the difference between reforming something and tearing it down?
Why might a writer let a fool say what he thinks, instead of saying it himself?

blocks.html: Thomas More's Utopia (1516), written by Erasmus's friend, plays a similar game: a traveler describes a perfect island, and readers are left to decide how seriously to take it. Rabelais and Montaigne, next on this ladder, both read Erasmus closely.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Folly says friends get along by overlooking each other's faults. Is that a good thing, or a kind of fib?
  2. Which group that Folly teases would you most like to tease, and why?
  3. How can you tell when someone is joking and when they mean it?
  4. Erasmus stayed in his church while criticizing it. When is it better to stay and speak up, and when to leave?
  5. Why do you think this little joke of a book became a best seller?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Machiavelli writes frankly about cruelty, deceit and war as tools of power. This lesson presents his arguments as his views, with the main criticisms, and quotes nothing graphic.

  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Niccolò Machiavelli worked for the city of Florence, in Italy, about five hundred years ago, as a kind of messenger and adviser who traveled to meet kings and generals. When the rulers of Florence changed, he lost his job. At home on his little farm, he wrote a short book called The Prince, full of advice for anyone who rules a country.

Most advice books of his time told rulers to be good, kind and honest. Machiavelli said: let us look at how rulers really act, and what really works. Some of his advice is wise, like getting ready for trouble before it comes. Some of it shocked people then and still does, like saying a ruler sometimes has to break his promises.

blocks.name: gb-fortune-river
blocks.cap: Machiavelli's picture: luck is like a river that floods. Build the dikes while the weather is calm.

blocks.html: Because of this book, people today call a sneaky, scheming person "Machiavellian." Whether that is fair to Machiavelli is one of the questions grown-ups still argue about.

🧩 Talk it over

Feared or loved? Machiavelli asks whether it is better for a leader to be loved or feared. Think of a good team captain, teacher or coach. Do people follow them because they like them, because they respect them, or because they are a little afraid of them? Make two lists, then talk about it: is there a third answer Machiavelli missed?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527) served the Republic of Florence for fourteen years as a secretary and diplomat, and met the hard men of his age, above all Cesare Borgia. In 1512 the Medici family returned to power, the republic fell, and Machiavelli was dismissed, briefly jailed and questioned under torture, then released. In 1513, living on his farm outside the city, he wrote The Prince and dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici, hoping for work. It was printed only in 1532, after his death.

Machiavelli's great move, in Chapter XV, is to say he will write about the real truth of things, how people actually live, rather than imagined ideal states. A prince who always tries to be good among so many who are not, he says, will come to ruin. So the prince must learn how to do wrong, and use that knowledge or not as necessity requires.

blocks.name: gb-principalities
blocks.cap: The book begins with a map of kinds of state. Tap each to see what Machiavelli says about it.

blocks.html: Read the whole chapter, though, and the picture is more careful. A prince must above all avoid being hated, and the surest way to be hated, he says, is to take people's property. Fear without hatred keeps a state stable; cruelty that breeds hatred destroys it.

In the same chapter he says a prince need not keep his word when keeping it would harm him, but must seem merciful, faithful, humane, upright and religious. This is the advice that made his name a byword for deceit.

Two words run through the book. Fortuna is chance, the turns of events no one controls. Virtù is not quite our "virtue": it is a ruler's skill, energy and nerve. In Chapter XXV he says that "Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions," leaving the other half, or a little less, to us, and compares her to a river in flood that does its worst where no dikes were built in calm weather.

blocks.title: Machiavelli's argument, laid out
blocks.q: Chapter XVII: why is it safer to be feared than loved?
steps: Premise: people are, in general, ungrateful and self-interested.
Premise: love is a bond of obligation, which people break when it suits them.
Premise: fear is kept up by the dread of punishment, which never fails.
Conclusion: so, if a prince must choose, being feared is safer, provided he is not hated.
blocks.a: The conclusion rests on a claim about human nature. To argue with Machiavelli, you can question that first premise.

blocks.text: How the book has been judged

head: Reading
The case for it
The case against it
rows: It openly advises cruelty and deceit "when necessary"; the Church banned it in 1559, and "Machiavellian" became a word for scheming.
It also insists on avoiding hatred, on laws and good arms, and on the common good of Italy.
Rousseau and others thought it exposed how tyrants work, so that free people could see it.
Machiavelli seems sincere in seeking a post from the Medici.
It studies power as it is, as later realists did.
Critics say it separates politics from morality too sharply.
blocks.cap: Three main readings (our summary). Scholars still debate them.

blocks.html: Machiavelli's longer Discourses on Livy, written about the same time, praises free republics where citizens share power, and many readers think it shows his deeper loyalties. The two books are best read together.

Assuming Machiavelli said "the end justifies the means." That phrase is not in The Prince. He did argue that a ruler will be judged by results, which is close, and readers disagree about how far he meant it.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

In Machiavelli's day Italy was divided into rival states, Florence, Venice, Milan, Naples and the Papal States among them, while France and Spain sent armies through it. The last chapter of The Prince is a passionate plea for a leader to unite Italy and drive the "barbarians" out. Some readers see the whole book as written toward that hope.

items: Should leaders be judged by the same rules as everyone else, or are there times when a ruler must do what an ordinary person should not?
Is Machiavelli right that people are mostly self-interested? What evidence would count for or against him?
Can fear keep order without becoming hatred? Where is the line?
How much of life is fortune, and how much is up to us?

blocks.html: Later books on this ladder answer him: Hobbes builds on a dark view of human nature; Locke, Montesquieu and the authors of the Federalist look for ways to limit rulers through laws and checks. Shakespeare's history plays, also in this era, show kings who live and die by Machiavelli's rules.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Is it better for a leader to be loved or feared? Can someone be both?
  2. Machiavelli says a ruler must sometimes break a promise. Is that ever right? Can you think of a case on each side?
  3. What "dikes" could you build now, in calm weather, against future trouble?
  4. Why do you think Machiavelli's name became a word for scheming? Is that fair?
  5. Should we judge an author by his worst advice or by his whole book?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

François Rabelais was a French monk who became a doctor, and he loved to laugh. He wrote a huge, silly story about a family of giants: Grandgousier, his son Gargantua, and Gargantua's son Pantagruel. The giants are so big that the story can get as wild as Rabelais likes.

Young Gargantua has terrible teachers at first, who make him memorize old books backward and forward. Then a good teacher takes him in hand. He learns by looking at the stars, plants and stones, playing games, making music and talking about what he has read. Rabelais was showing what good learning could be.

Later a hot-headed neighbor king, Picrochole, starts a war over some cakes. Gargantua's kind old father tries everything to make peace. After the war, Gargantua builds an abbey for his friend Friar John, the opposite of a strict monastery, with only one rule.

blocks.name: gb-theleme
blocks.cap: The Abbey of Thélème, drawn from Rabelais's description. Tap its parts.

blocks.html: For parents: Rabelais is famous for rude, earthy jokes. A good retelling for children, or the chosen chapters on Gargantua's education (Book I, chapters 14 to 24) and the Abbey of Thélème (chapters 52 to 57), suit young readers best.

🧩 Try this: draw a plan

Design your own abbey. Thélème had six towers, a fountain, libraries in many languages, and a single rule. Draw a plan for a school or clubhouse where people learn because they want to. What is your one rule? Where do you put the library?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

François Rabelais (c. 1494–1553) was a Franciscan and then a Benedictine monk, a student of Greek (a friend by letter of the great humanist scholars), and a doctor who practiced in Lyon. In 1532 he published Pantagruel, and about two years later Gargantua, about Pantagruel's father. Three more books followed, the last printed in 1564 after his death. He wrote in French, inventing words by the hundred.

head: Book
Date
Main story
rows: The birth, schooling and adventures of the giant Pantagruel, and his meeting with Panurge
Gargantua's education, the war with Picrochole, and the Abbey of Thélème
Panurge asks everyone whether he should marry
A sea voyage to strange islands in search of an oracle
The voyage's end (its authorship is debated)
blocks.cap: The five books.

blocks.html: Under the jokes lies a serious humanist program. Gargantua's first tutors stuff him with rote learning; his new tutor, Ponocrates, fills his day with reading, observing nature, exercise, music and conversation. In Pantagruel, Gargantua writes his son a famous letter urging him to master languages, history, mathematics, law, medicine and Scripture, and warning that "science without conscience" ruins the soul.

When shepherds and cake-sellers quarrel, King Picrochole marches out to conquer the world. Grandgousier, Gargantua's father, offers to pay damages and more, and fights only when he must. Rabelais is mocking wars of conquest and praising rulers who prefer peace, a theme Erasmus also preached.

As a reward, Friar John gets an abbey built to his own design: no walls, no clocks, men and women together, and anyone free to leave and marry. Rabelais describes its six towers, its libraries in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, French, Italian and Spanish, and its gardens. Then he gives its rule.

Thélème rests on a belief about people: that the well-taught and free, among good companions, will choose good on their own. It is the hope of humanist education. Whether it is wise, naive, or a joke at its own expense is for the reader to decide.
Reading "Do What Thou Wilt" as "do whatever you like, good or bad." Rabelais limits it to people already trained in honor, and his abbey is a picture of what education might make possible.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The theologians of the Sorbonne in Paris condemned his books, and Rabelais had to rely on powerful protectors. Some readers have called him a scoffer; others, a reforming Christian humanist who mocked only empty forms. Scholars still argue about his faith, and the books leave room for both views.

blocks.text: Laughter as a way of seeing

blocks.html: Rabelais mixes high learning with low comedy, lists that run for pages, and words he coins on the spot. The word "Rabelaisian" now means coarse, abundant humor. Later writers from Swift (Gulliver's giants and tiny people, later on this ladder) to the novelists of the 1700s learned from him how much a comic story can carry.

items: Would people really choose good if they were free and well taught, as Thélème assumes?
Why might someone put serious ideas inside a silly story?
Is a war over cakes any sillier than other wars? What is Rabelais saying about pride?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What would a school be like if its only rule were "do what you will"? Would it work for your family?
  2. Gargantua's good teacher used games, music and nature walks. What is the best way you have ever learned something?
  3. Grandgousier tried hard to avoid war. What does it take to keep the peace when someone wants a fight?
  4. Rabelais says laughing is part of being human. What makes something funny, and can a joke be wise?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Michel de Montaigne was a French nobleman who, at 38, decided to stop working for the government and spend his days in a round stone tower on his family's land, with a thousand books. He painted wise sayings on the wooden beams of the ceiling. Then he started writing.

He didn't write stories or poems. He wrote down his thoughts about everything: friendship, fear, children, cats, sleep, cannibals, smells, how to die and how to live. He called each piece an essai, French for "a try," because he was trying out his thoughts. That is where our word essay comes from.
Montaigne liked to look at both sides of a question. He even had a medal made with a pair of balanced scales and the words Que sais-je?, "What do I know?"

blocks.name: gb-scales
blocks.cap: Put reasons on each side of the scales, the way Montaigne liked to weigh a question.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this: an essai

Write a real essay, Montaigne's way. Choose a small topic you know well: your dog, rainy days, your favorite food, being the youngest. Write one page that tries out your thoughts. Say what you think, then say what someone else might think, and end with a question you still have.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) grew up speaking Latin, because his father had him taught it from birth, and became a magistrate in Bordeaux. In 1563 his dearest friend, Étienne de La Boétie, died young. In 1571 Montaigne retired to his tower library and began writing short pieces that grew into the Essays: Books I and II in 1580, Book III in 1588, with additions in the margins until he died. In between, he traveled to Italy and served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux, during France's bitter wars of religion.

This was new. Writers before him had written about God, nature, history or the soul. Montaigne made his own changing, ordinary self the subject, not to boast but because, he said, each person bears the whole form of the human condition.

In "Of the Education of Children" he asks for a tutor "who has rather a well-made than a well-filled head," one who will make the pupil "examine and thoroughly sift everything he reads," so that what is learned becomes the student's own.

blocks.text: Doubt, and what it is good for

blocks.html: Montaigne's longest essay, the "Apology for Raymond Sebond," piles up examples of how weak human reason is: our senses deceive us, wise men disagree, and customs that seem natural in one country seem absurd in another. He wonders whether, when he plays with his cat, the cat is not amusing herself with him more than he with her. This kind of thinking is called skepticism: holding back from firm judgment when the reasons are unclear.

For Montaigne, doubt was not despair. It made him slow to condemn, tolerant of other people's customs, and wary of the certainty that drove the religious wars around him. He remained a Catholic all his life, and saw no conflict between doubting human reason and keeping his faith.

In "Of Cannibals" he writes about the native people of Brazil he had read about and met. He argues that Europeans call barbarous whatever is not their own custom, and that the cruelties of his own country's wars were no better. It is one of the first essays to turn the questions a traveler asks back on his own society.
Montaigne's method: try out a thought, look at the other side, give examples from books and from your own life, and admit what you don't know. That is still a good definition of an essay.
Thinking an essay has to be stiff and formal. Montaigne's essays wander, change their minds and talk to the reader. The five-paragraph essay of school is a later, tidier cousin.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

John Florio translated the Essays into English in 1603, and Shakespeare seems to have read him: Gonzalo's dream of an ideal commonwealth in The Tempest borrows lines from "Of Cannibals." Charles Cotton's translation (1685), revised by Hazlitt in 1877, is the one quoted here. Francis Bacon, later on this ladder, borrowed the word "essay" for his own, much shorter pieces (1597).

His early essays lean on the ancient Stoics, as in "That to Study Philosophy is to Learn to Die," which argues that thinking about death in advance robs it of its terror. His later essays, especially the last, "Of Experience," grow gentler: learn to live well, enjoy the body and the day, and know yourself. Readers like to watch his mind change across twenty years.

items: Is writing about yourself a way of learning about everyone?
When is doubt wise, and when does it become an excuse not to decide?
Are some customs truly better than others, or only different? How would you judge?
What is the difference between a full head and a well-made one?

blocks.html: Pascal, on the next rung of this ladder, read Montaigne closely and argued with him, admiring his honesty and rejecting his ease with doubt. Descartes set out to defeat doubt with certainty.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Montaigne said "What do I know?" What is something you are not sure about, even though people expect you to be?
  2. If you wrote a book about yourself, what would be in the first chapter?
  3. Montaigne compared a good student to a bee that makes its own honey. How can you make what you learn your own?
  4. Is it fair to judge people from other places by our own customs? When might it be right to?
  5. Montaigne's best friend died young, and he wrote about friendship for the rest of his life. What makes a friendship last?

blocks.html: A note for parents: This lesson describes Calvin's religious teaching respectfully, as his own views, and gives the main points on which other Christians and later critics disagreed. It does not argue for or against any faith.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Five hundred years ago, many Christians in Europe were arguing about what the Church should teach and how it should be run. This time is called the Reformation. One of its leaders was a young Frenchman named John Calvin.

When Calvin was only 26, he wrote a book to explain, clearly and in order, what he believed the Bible teaches. He called it the Institutes of the Christian Religion. "Institutes" meant "instruction": a teaching book. He kept making it bigger and better for the rest of his life.

Calvin lived and worked in the city of Geneva, in Switzerland. His ideas spread to Scotland, the Netherlands, France and England, and later across the ocean with the Pilgrims and Puritans to America. Churches that follow his teaching are often called Reformed or Presbyterian.

blocks.name: gb-institutes
blocks.cap: The final Institutes is built in four parts. Tap each to see what it is about.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this: plan a book

Make a table of contents. Calvin organized his whole book in four parts, following an old Christian statement of belief called the Apostles' Creed. Pick something you know a lot about (a sport, a game, a hobby) and plan a book about it in four parts. What comes first? What comes last? Why?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

John Calvin (1509–1564) was born in Noyon, in northern France, studied law and the humanist classics, and around 1533 joined the movement for reform begun by Martin Luther. Protestants were being persecuted in France, so he left. In 1536, in Basel, he published the first Institutes, six chapters long, with a preface asking King Francis I to stop the persecution. That same year he was persuaded to stay in Geneva, and apart from a few years in Strasbourg he led its church until his death.

He revised the book again and again, in Latin and in French. His French version of 1541 is a landmark of French prose. The final Latin edition of 1559 has four books and eighty chapters. This lesson describes Calvin's teaching as Calvin's, in his own terms.

The argument runs both ways. Looking at our own weakness, Calvin says, drives us to look for God; and only by comparing ourselves with God's goodness do we see ourselves truly. The whole book unfolds from this pairing.

blocks.name: gb-institutes
blocks.cap: The 1559 Institutes, following the order of the Apostles' Creed.

head: Key idea
Calvin's teaching (as he states it)
rows: God is known dimly in creation, and clearly in the Bible, which is the final authority for faith.
God rules and cares for everything that happens.
Since Adam, human nature is deeply damaged by sin, and cannot save itself.
People are made right with God by grace through faith in Christ, not by earning it; good works follow as fruit.
God has chosen from eternity those who will be saved. Calvin calls this a comfort to believers and warns against prying into it.
The true church is where the Word is preached and the two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, are rightly given.
Rulers are appointed by God for order and justice and should be obeyed, though lesser magistrates may resist a tyrant, and God must be obeyed before any human ruler.
blocks.cap: Main teachings of the Institutes (our summary).

blocks.title: Counting the chapters
blocks.q: The four books of the 1559 Institutes have 18, 17, 25 and 20 chapters. How many chapters in all, and which book is longest?
steps: Book III, on faith and the Christian life, has the most: 25.
blocks.a: 80 chapters; Book III is the longest.

blocks.html: Calvin's teaching won wide followings and fierce opponents. Catholic theologians rejected his views on the church, the sacraments and justification. Among Protestants, Lutherans differed with him on the Lord's Supper, and from about 1600 the followers of Jacobus Arminius disputed his teaching on election, a debate that continues in churches today. Calvin's Geneva has been admired for its schools, its care for refugees and its orderly church, and criticized for its strict control of private life; the burning of the anti-Trinitarian Michael Servetus in 1553, which Calvin supported, has troubled readers from his own century on.

His influence reached far beyond theology. Reformed churches spread to Scotland (with John Knox), the Netherlands, Hungary and France (the Huguenots), and to England and New England with the Puritans. Historians still debate how much Calvinism shaped ideas of work, education and self-government in those lands.
Treating "Calvinism" as Calvin's teaching only about predestination. That is one doctrine among many in the Institutes, which Calvin placed late in Book III and handled with caution.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Calvin was trained as a humanist: his first book was a commentary on Seneca. He brought the humanist habits of going back to original sources, reading Greek and Hebrew, and writing clearly. The Institutes quotes Augustine more than any other writer after the Bible, and also cites Plato, Cicero and Seneca.

items: Calvin says knowing God and knowing ourselves depend on each other. Do you think self-knowledge needs something beyond the self?
How should a community balance shared rules with individual freedom of conscience?
What do people owe their rulers, and when, if ever, may they resist?

blocks.html: Earlier on this ladder, Augustine and Aquinas wrote the great systematic accounts of Christian teaching Calvin read and argued with. Later, Pascal (a Catholic writing against Calvin's Jesuit opponents and sometimes accused of being too close to Calvin) and Locke (on toleration and government) take up the questions he raised.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Calvin says true wisdom is knowing God and knowing ourselves. What do you think true wisdom is?
  2. Why do you think Calvin kept rewriting his book for twenty-three years?
  3. Calvin asked the King of France to stop persecuting people for their beliefs. Why is freedom of religion important?
  4. People disagreed fiercely about Calvin's ideas. How can people who disagree about deep questions still live together peacefully?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Every day the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. It really looks as if the sun goes around us. For a very long time, almost everyone believed the Earth stood still in the middle of everything, with the sun, moon, planets and stars circling it.

Nicolaus Copernicus was a church official and astronomer in Poland about 500 years ago. He had a bold idea: maybe the sun is in the middle, and the Earth is a planet that goes around it, spinning like a top once a day. The sun only looks like it moves, the way trees seem to slide past when you ride in a car.

His idea explained a strange puzzle. Mars usually creeps slowly eastward among the stars. But every two years or so it stops, goes backward for a few weeks, then goes forward again. Why? Copernicus said: because Earth is passing Mars, like a faster runner on an inside track. From the fast runner, the slow one seems to slide backward for a while.

blocks.cap: Press Play. Earth (blue) laps Mars (red). The dashed line shows where we see Mars among the stars. Watch the orange marks: Mars seems to go backward while Earth passes it.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Be the planets. Put a lamp or a ball in the middle of a room for the sun. One person walks slowly in a big circle (Mars). Another walks faster in a smaller circle inside (Earth), always looking at "Mars" and noticing what is on the wall behind it. When Earth passes Mars, what does the wall behind Mars seem to do?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543) was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland. He studied at Kraków, then in Italy at Bologna, Padua and Ferrara, where he took a doctorate in canon (church) law. For most of his life he was a canon of the cathedral at Frombork, managing church lands, practicing medicine and, in his spare hours, observing the sky. Around 1510 he passed around a short handwritten sketch of a sun-centered system, the Commentariolus. His full book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, came out in Nuremberg in 1543, the year he died.

Astronomy had followed Claudius Ptolemy's Almagest (about AD 150) for 1,400 years. Ptolemy put the Earth at the center. Each planet rode on a small circle, the epicycle, whose center moved around a large circle, the deferent. To match the planets' changing speeds, Ptolemy also measured the motion as even not around the deferent's center but around another point, the equant. It worked well enough to predict positions, but Copernicus thought the equant broke the rule that heavenly motions should be uniform circles, and that the system did not hang together as one design.

blocks.text: Idea 1: the sun at the center, the Earth in motion

blocks.html: Book I sets out the new order. The Earth turns on its axis once a day, which makes the whole sky seem to wheel around us. The Earth goes around the sun once a year, which makes the sun seem to move through the zodiac. The planets, in order from the sun, are Mercury, Venus, Earth (with the Moon going around it), Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. The stars are so far away that the Earth's yearly motion causes no shift we can see in them.

In Ptolemy's system, each planet's backward loop (its retrograde motion) needed its own epicycle, timed just so. In Copernicus's system, the loops come free: they are what we see when the faster Earth overtakes an outer planet, or when an inner planet overtakes us. And it explains a coincidence Ptolemy could only accept: the outer planets loop backward exactly when they are opposite the sun in our sky.

blocks.name: gb-sky
blocks.cap: The same motion, drawn with Earth held still. Mars rides an epicycle (dashed) on a deferent (purple). The epicycle turns once a year and is the same size as Earth's orbit: Ptolemy's epicycle for an outer planet is Earth's own orbit in disguise. Switch views to compare, and try "In our sky" for the backward loop.

blocks.text: Idea 3: a system whose parts fit

blocks.html: The biggest gain was not accuracy but order. In Ptolemy's scheme each planet was a separate model; nothing fixed how far away each was. In Copernicus's, the sizes of the planets' orbits follow from what we see, and the planets fall into order: the farther from the sun, the slower they go.

blocks.title: How far is Venus from the sun?
blocks.q: Venus never strays more than about $46°$ from the sun in our sky (its greatest elongation). If the orbits are circles, how far is Venus from the sun, with Earth's distance as 1?
steps: At greatest elongation, the line from Earth just touches Venus's orbit, so the angle at Venus is a right angle.
blocks.a: About 0.72 of Earth's distance, very close to the modern value of 0.723.

blocks.title: How often does Mars loop?
blocks.q: Earth goes around the sun in 1 year; Mars takes 1.88 years. How often does Earth lap Mars (the time between loops)?
steps: Each year Earth gains $1 - \frac{1}{1.88}$ of a lap on Mars.

items: Copernicus did not get rid of epicycles. Old textbooks say his system was much simpler. In fact, to match the observations he still used small circles on circles, about as many as the Ptolemaic models of his day. What his system dropped was the big epicycles used for the backward loops, and the equant. The story that Ptolemy's followers had piled up "80 epicycles on epicycles" is a later myth; the historian Owen Gingerich showed that the tables astronomers actually used came from Ptolemy's simple models.

It was not more accurate at first. Tables made from Copernicus's book (the Prutenic Tables of 1551) predicted planet positions about as well as the old tables. Real gains came with Tycho Brahe's far better observations and Kepler's ellipses.

The unsigned preface. The book opened with a short note, "To the Reader", saying the new system was only a way to calculate, not a claim about the real world. Copernicus did not write it; the Lutheran minister Andreas Osiander, who oversaw the printing, added it without signing it. Kepler later made this public.

Not banned at once. The book was read and taught for seventy years. In 1616, during the controversy around Galileo, the Catholic Church's Congregation of the Index suspended it "until corrected"; a list of corrections followed in 1620. People of different churches and none argued for and against it, on scientific as well as religious grounds: no one could yet detect the Earth's motion directly.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the sun near the center of the planets' motions, the Earth as a planet that spins daily and orbits yearly, the order and relative distances of the planets, and the explanation of backward loops. Changed: Kepler replaced the circles with ellipses (1609) and threw out the epicycles for good. Newton explained the motions with gravity, and showed that the sun and planets actually circle their common center of mass, which lies near the sun. The stars are not fixed on a sphere: they are suns, at vastly different distances, and the yearly shift of the nearest one (stellar parallax) was finally measured by Friedrich Bessel in 1838.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Two descriptions, one motion. The visual above shows something surprising: for a single planet, a sun-centered circle plus Earth's circle and an Earth-centered deferent plus epicycle can trace exactly the same path. So which is "true"? The case for Copernicus was not that his geometry fit one planet better, but that one arrangement explained them all at once, and fixed their distances. Choosing a theory because it ties many facts together is a big part of how science judges ideas.

Common sense and motion. If the Earth spins, why don't we feel a wind, or why doesn't a dropped stone land behind us? Copernicus had only partial answers. Galileo's work on motion (Two New Sciences, on this ladder) supplied the idea that we share the Earth's motion and so do not notice it.

Reading the dedication. Copernicus writes to Pope Paul III, mentions the cardinal and the bishop who urged him to publish, and says his book has waited "not nine years merely, but already going on four times nine." Why might he have waited so long? Read his own explanation and form your own view.
Big questions. When our senses and a theory disagree, which should we trust? Is a simpler explanation more likely to be true, or only easier to use?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. It looks as if the sun moves across the sky. What other things look one way but turn out to be another?
  2. Why do you think Copernicus waited so many years before publishing?
  3. Someone added a preface to Copernicus's book saying it was only a way to calculate. Is it fair to add words to someone else's book? Why might the editor have done it?
  4. Copernicus's system was not more accurate at first. Why might people still have found it worth taking seriously?
  5. Walk the planets in your living room. Can you see the backward loop yourselves?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, in 1564. He went to London, became an actor, and wrote about 38 plays and many poems. Four hundred years later, people all over the world still act them.

His comedies are not just jokes. They are stories where everything gets mixed up and then comes right at the end, usually with a wedding (or three). In A Midsummer Night's Dream, four young people run away into an enchanted wood. A mischievous fairy named Puck uses a magic flower to make people fall in love with the wrong person, and gives a weaver named Bottom a donkey's head!

blocks.html: Shakespeare's plays were acted in an open-air theater called the Globe. Some people sat in covered galleries. Others paid a penny to stand in the yard right next to the stage.

🧩 Try this: a play with people as scenery

Put on a scene. The workmen in A Midsummer Night's Dream put on a play so badly that it becomes a comedy: one of them plays a wall, and another plays the moonshine. Choose a simple story (the three little pigs, perhaps) and act it with your family, with people playing the scenery too. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was a glover's son from Stratford-upon-Avon. By the early 1590s he was in London as an actor and playwright, and from 1594 he was a member and part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men. In 1599 the company built the Globe on the south bank of the Thames. Plays were acted in daylight, with little scenery and with boys in the women's parts. In 1623, seven years after his death, two fellow actors gathered 36 of his plays in the First Folio.

Disguise and mistaken identity, especially women dressed as young men.
A wise fool who sees more than the lords.
Love that runs into obstacles, and an ending in marriages and forgiveness.

blocks.html: Three worlds meet in the wood: the young Athenian lovers, the fairy court of Oberon and Titania, and the "rude mechanicals," workmen rehearsing a play for the Duke's wedding. Puck's mistakes with the love-flower make the lovers swap and quarrel. The fairy queen, under the same spell, falls in love with Bottom. By morning, all is set right.
Notice the rhythm: the fairies often speak in short, chanting, rhymed lines, while the lovers speak in longer verse and the workmen in prose. Shakespeare gives each world its own music.
Jaques goes on to describe the "seven ages" of a life, from infant to old age. It is a melancholy speech in a happy play, and a good example of how the comedies make room for sadness too.

Thinking a comedy must be all jokes. In Shakespeare, "comedy" means a story that moves from trouble to harmony. Several comedies have dark moments, and The Merchant of Venice has troubled many modern readers for how it treats Shylock, its Jewish moneylender.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Rosalind, Viola and Portia are among the cleverest people in their plays, and all three spend much of the play dressed as young men. On Shakespeare's stage, where boys played women, this meant a boy playing a woman playing a man. Readers still discuss what the disguises let these heroines say and do.

items: Why do comedies so often take people out of the city and into a forest?
Is love in Shakespeare's comedies a kind of madness, a kind of wisdom, or both?
Why does Shakespeare end so many plays with forgiveness?

blocks.html: Earlier on this ladder, Aristophanes wrote the comedies of ancient Athens; Erasmus's Folly speaks like Shakespeare's wise fools. Later, Molière's comedies in France take up the same tangles of love and pretense.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Puck says "Lord, what fools these mortals be!" When have you seen people act foolishly because of love or friendship?
  2. Why do you think so many of Shakespeare's heroines wear disguises?
  3. If you could stand in the Globe's yard for a penny, would you? What would be fun about it, and what would not?
  4. Jaques says all the world's a stage. What part are you playing right now?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
In the Italian city of Verona live two families, the Montagues and the Capulets, who have hated each other for so long that no one remembers why. Their servants even fight in the street.

Romeo, a Montague, sneaks into a Capulet party and meets Juliet, a Capulet. They fall in love at once, before they even learn each other's names. Then, at night, Juliet stands at her window and wonders aloud why a name should matter so much.

They marry in secret, hoping to end the feud. But a street fight, a hasty choice, and a letter that never arrives lead to a sad ending: both young people die. Only then do their families, heartbroken, make peace.

For parents: the play has sword fights and ends with the deaths of the two young lovers by their own hands. Young readers can follow the story through Act II (the meeting, the balcony and the secret wedding) and a good retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

🧩 Try this: change one choice

Slow down. Friar Laurence warns Romeo, "Wisely, and slow. They stumble that run fast." List every choice in the story that was made in a hurry. Then rewrite one of them: what if someone had waited a day?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet around 1595, early in his career. He took the plot from Arthur Brooke's long English poem The Tragical History of Romeus and Juliet (1562), which came from Italian tales. He sped the story up from months to about four days, and gave the minor characters, Mercutio and the Nurse, unforgettable life.

The prologue is a sonnet, fourteen lines rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, and it tells us the ending before the play begins. We watch knowing what the characters do not: this is dramatic irony, and it makes every hopeful moment ache.

blocks.html: When Romeo and Juliet first speak, their fourteen lines together make another sonnet, shared between them. Later, at her window, he compares her to the sun.

blocks.cap: Tap out the beat of Romeo's line, and compare it with others.

blocks.html: The play turns in Act III. Mercutio, Romeo's friend, is killed by Tybalt; Romeo, in a rage, kills Tybalt and is banished. From then on, chance and haste work together: a forced engagement to Paris, the Friar's risky potion, a plague that stops his letter, and Romeo arriving at the tomb minutes too soon. Readers still argue whether the lovers are destroyed by fate ("star-cross'd"), by their own speed, or by the hatred of their elders.

Calling the play a simple love story. It is also about a city poisoned by an old feud, and about how young people pay for their elders' hatred. Juliet is not yet fourteen, and the adults around her mostly fail her.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: A tragedy that starts as a comedy

blocks.html: The first two acts have the stuff of comedy: a party, a balcony, a witty friend, a comic Nurse, a secret wedding. Then Mercutio dies, and the play turns. Critics see Shakespeare testing what happens when comedy's young lovers meet a world that will not bend.

items: Is it fate, chance, or choice that destroys the lovers?
Is their love wise, or only young? Does it matter?
Why does it take a disaster to end the feud? Who is most to blame?

blocks.html: Ovid's tale of Pyramus and Thisbe, two lovers separated by their parents, is an ancestor of this play, and Shakespeare mocked it lovingly in A Midsummer Night's Dream, written at about the same time.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Juliet asks "What's in a name?" Can a name, or a family, make someone your enemy?
  2. Who is most to blame for what happens: Romeo, Juliet, their parents, the Friar, or bad luck?
  3. Friar Laurence says "They stumble that run fast." When has hurrying caused you trouble?
  4. Why do you think the play tells us the ending in its very first speech?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Shakespeare wrote ten plays about the kings of England who lived one to two hundred years before him. They are full of crowns, battles, plots and speeches. Together they tell how England's kings lost the crown, fought for it, and finally made peace.

The most famous young hero is Prince Hal. He spends his days in a tavern with a fat, funny, boastful knight named Sir John Falstaff, and everyone thinks Hal will be a terrible king. But when he becomes King Henry V, he leads a small, tired English army to victory at the Battle of Agincourt.

blocks.name: gb-kings
blocks.cap: The kings from Richard II to Henry VII, and the plays about them. Tap a king.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this: a rallying speech

Rally the team. Before battle, Henry V gives speeches to cheer his soldiers. Write a short speech to cheer up a team before a big game or a hard test. Use "we" a lot, and end with a line people will remember.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

In the 1590s Shakespeare wrote two linked groups of four plays. The first, written first, covers the later story: the three parts of Henry VI and Richard III, from the loss of France through the Wars of the Roses to the Battle of Bosworth (1485). The second, often called the Henriad, goes back to the beginning: Richard II, Henry IV Parts 1 and 2, and Henry V. He also wrote King John and, near the end of his career, Henry VIII with John Fletcher.

blocks.name: gb-kings
blocks.cap: Reigns by royal house. The shaded band marks the Wars of the Roses.

blocks.html: His main source was Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles (1587). He compressed years into scenes, invented speeches and characters (Falstaff above all), and shaped history into drama. His audience lived under Elizabeth I, granddaughter of Henry VII, the Tudor who won at Bosworth, so the plays' ending in Tudor peace mattered to them.

Richard II believes a king rules by God's right and cannot be touched. His cousin Henry Bolingbroke, whom he has exiled and robbed, comes back with an army and takes the throne as Henry IV. Before that, the dying John of Gaunt mourns what England has become.

blocks.text: Henry IV: the tavern and the throne

blocks.html: Henry IV's reign is troubled by rebellion and by guilt over how he took the crown. His son Hal seems to waste his youth with Falstaff, a witty, cowardly, lovable old knight. Hal tells the audience early on that he is biding his time. He proves himself at the Battle of Shrewsbury, and when he becomes king he publicly rejects Falstaff. Readers have argued ever since whether that is wise statesmanship or a cold betrayal of a friend.

The Chorus asks the audience to imagine armies and oceans on a small wooden stage. Henry invades France and, at Agincourt in 1415, defeats a much larger army. The play celebrates him, yet it also shows the cost of war: hanged friends, frightened soldiers, and a king who wonders, alone at night, what he owes the men who die for him.

At the far end of the story, Richard of Gloucester schemes and kills his way to the throne, letting the audience in on every plan. He is defeated at Bosworth by Henry Tudor. Historians have long debated how much of this dark portrait is fair, since it came from Tudor writers with reasons to blacken him.
Treating the plays as accurate history. They are dramas based on chronicles, written to move and entertain. They are best read alongside a good history of the period.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The history plays keep asking: is a king made by birth, by God, by ability, or by the consent of the people? Richard II has the right but not the skill; Henry IV has the skill but not the right; Henry V seems to have both, yet the plays show what his greatness costs. Machiavelli's The Prince, earlier in this era, asks the same questions in prose.

items: Is it ever right to remove a bad ruler by force?
Was Hal right to reject Falstaff? What does a leader owe old friends?
Can a play about war celebrate courage without celebrating war?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Prince Hal surprises everyone by becoming a great king. Have you ever been underestimated?
  2. Henry V calls his soldiers "dear friends." What makes people willing to follow a leader?
  3. Was it fair of Henry V to turn his back on Falstaff?
  4. Why might a playwright change history to tell a better story? Is that all right?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Long ago in Rome, a great general named Julius Caesar became so powerful that some Romans feared he would make himself king. A group of senators, led by Cassius and Caesar's friend Brutus, plotted to stop him.

On the Ides of March, the 15th, they killed him. Brutus told the crowd he had done it to keep Rome free. Then Caesar's friend Mark Antony gave a speech so clever that the crowd turned against the plotters. A war followed, and the plotters lost.
Shakespeare found this true story in a book by the Greek writer Plutarch, who lived about 1,500 years before him.

🧩 Try this: reason or feeling?

Two speeches. After the murder, Brutus speaks plainly and asks the crowd to think. Antony speaks with feeling and shows them Caesar's cloak. Pick a simple question (should we get a dog?) and give two short speeches, one with reasons only and one with feelings. Which persuades your family more?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Shakespeare wrote Julius Caesar in 1599; a Swiss visitor, Thomas Platter, saw it acted on Bankside that September, probably at the new Globe. His source was Plutarch's Lives of Caesar, Brutus and Antony, in Thomas North's English translation (1579), on an earlier rung of this ladder. The real murder took place in 44 BC.

blocks.cap: The five acts. The title character dies in the middle of the play.

blocks.html: Cassius works on Brutus with arguments and with forged letters from "citizens." Brutus, a man of honor, decides alone in his orchard that Caesar must die, not for what he is but for what power might make him. Readers have argued ever since whether Brutus is a hero of liberty, a traitor to a friend, or a good man who reasons himself into a terrible act.

Brutus speaks first, in prose, and appeals to the crowd's reason and to his own honor: "Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more." Then he lets Antony speak, against Cassius's advice. Antony, in verse, praises Brutus as "an honourable man" again and again until the phrase turns bitter, shows the crowd Caesar's wounds and cloak, and reads his will. The crowd riots.

blocks.html: Later Shakespeare returned to Plutarch for Antony and Cleopatra (c. 1606), the love and fall of Mark Antony and the queen of Egypt, and Coriolanus (c. 1608), a proud general of early Rome who scorns the people. These plays deal with mature themes; the summaries here are enough for young readers.
Thinking Caesar is the hero because the play has his name. Brutus has far more lines, and many critics see him as the tragic hero.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Julius Caesar shows how speech moves crowds, and how easily. Aristotle's Rhetoric, earlier on this ladder, names the tools both men use. The play stays neutral between them: Brutus is right that persuasion should be reasoned, and wrong about what moves people.

items: Can it ever be right to kill a leader to protect a republic? What does the play suggest, and what do you think?
Is Cassius right that the fault is "in ourselves" and not in fate?
Why does reason lose to feeling in the Forum? Should it?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Brutus says he loved Rome more than Caesar. Can loyalty to a cause ever be more important than loyalty to a friend?
  2. Who gave the better speech, Brutus or Antony? Which was more honest?
  3. Cassius says "The fault ... is not in our stars, / But in ourselves." Do you agree?
  4. Why do you think crowds can change their minds so quickly?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Prince Hamlet of Denmark comes home from university because his father, the King, has died. Worse, his uncle Claudius has become king and married Hamlet's mother, all in a few weeks. Hamlet is heartbroken.

Then, on the castle walls at midnight, a ghost appears: it looks like his father. It tells Hamlet that Claudius murdered him, and asks Hamlet to set things right. But is the ghost telling the truth? Hamlet decides to find out. He pretends to be a little mad, and he has some traveling actors put on a play that shows a murder like his father's, while he watches his uncle's face.

blocks.cap: Who is who in the castle of Elsinore. Tap a name.

blocks.html: Hamlet is famous because he thinks so hard about everything: about whether to act, about life and death, about what people are. His speeches have become some of the most quoted words in English.

For parents: Hamlet is a revenge tragedy, and most of the main characters die by the end. Young readers can follow Acts I and II (the ghost, the madness and the actors) and a good retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

🧩 Talk it over

Test the ghost. Hamlet cannot be sure the ghost is honest, so he sets a test. If you had to find out whether someone was telling the truth, without asking them, what test would you design? Is it fair to test people that way?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Hamlet (c. 1600) is Shakespeare's longest play and probably his most discussed. He took the old story of a Danish prince's revenge, known from a Danish chronicle of about 1200 and an earlier English play now lost, and turned it into a play about thinking, doubt and grief. It survives in three early versions (printed 1603, 1604 and 1623), which differ.

blocks.html: Hamlet promises revenge at the end of Act I and does not achieve it until the last scene. Why? He is not sure the Ghost is honest; it might be a devil in his father's shape. He blames himself for thinking too much. He spares Claudius at prayer for fear of sending his soul to heaven. Each explanation fits some scenes, and readers have argued for four hundred years.

blocks.text: To be, or not to be

blocks.html: In this soliloquy (a speech alone, thinking aloud) Hamlet weighs whether life's suffering is worth bearing, and concludes that fear of what may come after death keeps people going, and that too much thinking makes us slow to act. It is a speech about a question, not a decision.

blocks.html: The speech sums up the Renaissance praise of human greatness, and Hamlet, in his grief, can no longer feel it. That gap between what he knows and what he feels is the heart of the play.

Hamlet kills Polonius by mistake, is sent away, escapes, and returns calmer, ready to let things come. A fencing match with Laertes, rigged by Claudius with a poisoned blade and a poisoned cup, ends with the deaths of the Queen, Laertes, Claudius and Hamlet. Hamlet asks Horatio to live and tell his story, and the Norwegian prince Fortinbras takes the crown.

Thinking Hamlet is simply weak or indecisive. He acts boldly at times (the play, the escape at sea). The play asks harder questions: how to act rightly when you cannot be sure, and whether revenge can ever set the world right.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Hamlet, Laertes and Fortinbras have all lost fathers. Laertes rushes to revenge and is used by Claudius; Fortinbras acts without a second thought; Hamlet thinks. Shakespeare sets them side by side and lets us compare.

items: Can we ever be certain enough to act? What should we do when we are not?
Is revenge justice, or does it only make more wrongs?
Is Hamlet's madness real, pretended, or both?
What does Hamlet learn by the end, when he says "the readiness is all"?

blocks.html: Montaigne's Essays, on this ladder, share Hamlet's habit of doubt, and many scholars think Shakespeare read them. Sophocles' Oedipus, earlier, is another tragedy of a man who must discover a hidden crime.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Hamlet cannot be sure the ghost is telling the truth. What should you do when you cannot be sure?
  2. Is it better to think carefully before acting, or to act quickly? When is each one right?
  3. Polonius says "to thine own self be true." What does that mean to you?
  4. Hamlet asks Horatio to tell his story. Why does it matter to him that someone tells it truly?

This lesson summarizes the plot without detail, quotes none of the insults, and explains how readers have discussed the play's treatment of race.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Othello is a great general who serves the city of Venice. He is brave, honest and trusting, and he has married Desdemona, who loves him for the stories of his adventures.

But one of his officers, Iago, secretly hates him. Iago smiles, gives friendly advice, and everyone calls him "honest Iago." Bit by bit, with lies and a stolen handkerchief, he makes Othello believe that Desdemona loves someone else. The play shows how jealousy, once it starts, can grow like a monster.

blocks.name: gb-cast
blocks.cap: Follow the lines from Iago: he works on almost everyone.

blocks.html: For parents: Othello ends with Desdemona's murder by her husband and other deaths. Young readers can talk about the play's ideas (trust, lies and jealousy) through a retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

🧩 Try this: watch a rumor grow

The rumor game. Whisper a short, true sentence around a circle, each person adding one small change that sounds true. Compare the last version with the first. How did a small lie grow? How could you check a story before believing it?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Shakespeare wrote Othello around 1603–1604, from an Italian tale by Giraldi Cinthio (1565). It is one of his tightest tragedies: after Act I in Venice, the action moves to Cyprus, the enemy fleet is destroyed by a storm, and the danger moves inside, into one man's mind.

blocks.name: gb-acts
blocks.cap: The five acts.

blocks.html: Iago gives several reasons for his hatred: Othello promoted Cassio instead of him; he suspects, without evidence, other wrongs. The reasons shift, and the poet Coleridge called his soliloquies "the motive-hunting of a motiveless malignity." Iago tells the audience his plans, so we watch, knowing, as he works on Roderigo, Cassio, Othello and even his own wife.
The irony is sharp: Iago, praising a good name, is destroying Desdemona's. The word "honest" is used of him again and again.

Othello is a Moor, an African-born general who has served Venice all his life and is honored by its Senate. Desdemona's father objects to the marriage, and Iago and Roderigo use crude insults about Othello's origins. The play shows that prejudice, and many readers think it questions it: Othello is the noblest figure in the play until Iago's lies unmake him. How the play treats race has been discussed by readers and performers for centuries.

The handkerchief, Othello's first gift to Desdemona, becomes the false "proof." Emilia picks it up and gives it to Iago, who plants it with Cassio. In Act V, Othello kills Desdemona; Emilia, learning the truth, reveals her husband's plot; Othello, seeing what he has done, takes his own life. Iago refuses to explain himself.
Thinking Othello is foolish to believe Iago. Everyone in the play trusts Iago. The tragedy is how a good, trusting person can be turned by someone who knows exactly where to press.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Why do people believe lies that fit their fears?
Does Iago need a reason to do evil? What does it mean that he will not give one?
How should a play about prejudice be performed today?
What could Othello have done to test what he was told?

blocks.html: Iago, who smiles while he plots, is a cousin of the princes Machiavelli describes, who must seem honest while being a fox. Milton's Satan, later on this ladder, is another persuader who works on trust.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think everyone trusted Iago?
  2. Iago calls jealousy a "green-ey'd monster." Why is jealousy so hard to stop once it starts?
  3. How can you tell whether something you hear about a friend is true?
  4. Iago says a good name is worth more than money. Do you agree?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

King Lear of ancient Britain is old and wants to rest. He decides to divide his kingdom among his three daughters, and asks each to say how much she loves him. The two eldest, Goneril and Regan, flatter him with grand words. The youngest, Cordelia, who loves him most, will not.

Lear is furious and sends Cordelia away. Soon the flattering daughters turn him out of their homes, and he goes out into a terrible storm with only his Fool and a few loyal friends. In the storm, the proud king learns what it is to be poor and cold, and at last he sees which daughter truly loved him.

blocks.html: For parents: King Lear is one of Shakespeare's saddest plays and includes a cruel scene in which Gloucester is blinded, and the deaths of Cordelia and Lear. Young readers can follow Act I (the love test) and the reunion of Lear and Cordelia (Act IV, scene 7) or a retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

🧩 Talk it over

Love in words or deeds? Goneril and Regan say beautiful things; Cordelia says "Nothing" but loves her father. Make two lists: ways people show love with words, and ways they show it with actions. Which list is longer in your family?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Shakespeare wrote King Lear around 1605–1606, from the legend of a king of pre-Roman Britain told in Holinshed and an older play. He added a second family, the Earl of Gloucester and his two sons, whose story mirrors Lear's, and gave it an ending darker than any of his sources. It survives in two versions (1608 and 1623) that differ in many lines.

blocks.name: gb-acts
blocks.cap: The five acts.

blocks.html: Lear wants to be loved in words, in public, and to keep the honor of a king without its work. Cordelia's "Love, and be silent" is an aside to herself; she will love and obey "according to my bond." Kent, who defends her, is banished too, and returns in disguise to serve Lear.

Shut out by Goneril and Regan, Lear rages in the storm on the heath with his Fool, who tells him the truth in jokes, and with Edgar, Gloucester's loyal son, disguised as "Poor Tom," a beggar. Lear's mind gives way, and in his madness he sees more clearly than before: he pities the "poor naked wretches" he never thought of as king.

head: Lear's family
Gloucester's family
blocks.cap: The double plot.

blocks.html: Gloucester, for helping Lear, is cruelly punished and loses his sight. Led by Edgar, whom he does not recognize, he learns to "see" his son's loyalty. In Act IV, Cordelia returns with an army from France, and Lear wakes in her care and knows her. In Act V, her army is defeated, Edgar defeats Edmund, Goneril and Regan destroy each other, Cordelia is killed, and Lear dies with her in his arms.

The ending so troubled audiences that from 1681 to the 1830s theaters played Nahum Tate's rewrite, in which Cordelia lives and marries Edgar. Samuel Johnson, later on this ladder, said he could hardly bear to reread the last scenes.
Reading Lear's madness as only a loss. In the storm Lear becomes kinder and wiser than he ever was on the throne. The play asks whether suffering can teach what power could not.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Is the world of King Lear just? Do the gods, as some characters say, care at all?
Why does Lear need to hear love spoken? Why can't Cordelia say it?
What does it mean that the Fool and the madman are the wisest people on the heath?
Is the ending a cruel accident, or does it mean something?

blocks.html: Sophocles' Oedipus, earlier on this ladder, also loses his sight and learns the truth; the Book of Job asks why the good suffer. Dostoevsky's Brothers Karamazov, later, returns to fathers, children and the question of justice.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think Lear believed the flattering daughters?
  2. Cordelia could have saved herself with a few kind words. Was she right to refuse?
  3. The Fool tells Lear the truth with jokes. Why is it sometimes easier to hear hard truths that way?
  4. In the storm Lear thinks about poor people for the first time. What helps people understand others' troubles?

Choose a path

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

On a stormy Scottish heath, three strange witches meet a brave general named Macbeth and tell him he will be king. Macbeth can't stop thinking about it. His wife, Lady Macbeth, wants it too, and pushes him on.

Macbeth does a terrible thing to become king. But one wrong leads to another, and the Macbeths can't sleep or rest. Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep, trying to wash away a spot that isn't there. In the end, the good lords of Scotland gather an army, and the rightful prince becomes king.

blocks.html: For parents: Macbeth is a play about murder and guilt, with witches, ghosts and battles. It is short and gripping for older children, but some scenes are frightening. Young readers can start with Act I (the witches and the prophecy) and a retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

🧩 Try this: a witches' chant

Chant like a witch. The witches speak in short lines with a strong DUM-da beat. Write four lines in that beat about something ordinary ("Dishes, dishes, in the sink, / Pots and pans and things that stink") and chant them together.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Macbeth (c. 1606) is Shakespeare's shortest tragedy. It is drawn from Holinshed's account of an 11th-century Scottish king, much changed. Shakespeare wrote it soon after King James VI of Scotland became James I of England; James had written a book about witchcraft and claimed descent from Banquo, whom the play treats with honor.

blocks.cap: The five acts.

blocks.html: Macbeth knows the murder is wrong: Duncan is his king, his kinsman and his guest, and a good ruler. Lady Macbeth questions his courage and his love, and he goes ahead. Before the deed he sees a dagger in the air.

Each crime leads to the next. Macbeth has Banquo killed and sees his ghost at a feast; he has Macduff's family killed. Lady Macbeth, once the stronger, walks in her sleep trying to wash invisible blood from her hands. By the end Macbeth feels almost nothing, and he speaks of life as a tale "signifying nothing."

Macbeth thinks it means

blocks.html: The witches never tell Macbeth to murder anyone. They only say what will be. The play leaves open how much is fate and how much is his choice, and that question drives it.
Blaming the witches or Lady Macbeth for everything. Macbeth is told the future, and urged by his wife, but every choice is his, and he knows it.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Macbeth is full of images of blood, sleep, darkness and clothes that do not fit (borrowed robes, a giant's robe on a small man). The witches speak in a chanting trochaic beat, unlike anyone else; "fair is foul" turns up again in Macbeth's first line. Tracing these patterns is a good way to read the play closely.

items: If you were told you would get something you wanted, would you wait for it or try to make it happen?
Can a guilty conscience be escaped?
What makes a ruler a tyrant? How does the play show the difference between Duncan, Macbeth and Malcolm?

blocks.html: Machiavelli's chapter on those who rise "by wickedness" (The Prince, Chapter VIII) is a good companion: such men, he says, may win power but not glory.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. The witches tell Macbeth what will happen, but not what to do. Who is responsible for what Macbeth does?
  2. Why do you think one wrong act led Macbeth to another?
  3. Lady Macbeth was braver than her husband at first, but guilt overcame her. What does guilt feel like, and what is it good for?
  4. The witches say "Fair is foul, and foul is fair." When can something look good but be bad?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

On a magical island live a magician named Prospero, his daughter Miranda, an airy spirit called Ariel, and a creature named Caliban. Twelve years ago, Prospero's brother stole his dukedom in Italy and set him and baby Miranda adrift in a boat. They washed up here.

Now a ship carrying Prospero's old enemies sails near. Prospero raises a great storm, a tempest, and the ship is wrecked, but Ariel makes sure no one is hurt. On the island, the king's son meets Miranda and they fall in love. Prospero could take his revenge. Instead, he chooses to forgive.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this: map the island

Set Ariel free. At the end Prospero frees Ariel and gives up his magic. If you had one magic power for a day, what would you do with it, and what would you choose to give up afterward? Draw the island and mark where each character lives.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Late in his career, around 1608–1611, Shakespeare wrote four plays now often called romances: Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale and The Tempest. They share sea voyages, lost children found again, long years of separation, wonders, and forgiveness. The Tempest, probably the last play he wrote alone, was printed first in the First Folio.

head: Play
What is lost
What is found
rows: A prince's wife and baby daughter
A princess's good name and two brothers stolen as babies
A jealous king's wife and baby daughter
His dukedom, and a marriage that unites old enemies
blocks.cap: The romances.

blocks.cap: The five acts. The whole story takes about one afternoon.

blocks.html: Prospero controls everything on the island through his magic and Ariel's help. He brings his enemies to the edge of despair, and then, at the turn of Act V, he chooses mercy.

He forgives his brother Antonio, the King of Naples and the others, frees Ariel, and says he will break his staff and drown his book of magic. In the epilogue he steps forward and asks the audience to set him free with their applause.

Prospero speaks after ending a magical show for the young couple. The whole world, he says, will one day fade like a play. Many readers have heard in it Shakespeare's own farewell to the theater, though no one can prove that.

Caliban says the island was his until Prospero came and made him a servant. Prospero says he taught Caliban and was repaid with betrayal. Since the 1800s and especially in the last century, readers and directors have discussed the play in light of European voyages and colonies, while others read Caliban mainly as a figure of untaught nature. The play gives Caliban some of its most beautiful lines about the island's music.
Thinking Prospero is simply good. He is also harsh and controlling, and the play lets us see it. His choice to forgive matters because he could do otherwise.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Shakespeare seems to have read accounts of a 1609 shipwreck in Bermuda, and he borrowed from Montaigne's "Of Cannibals" (in Florio's 1603 translation) for Gonzalo's dream of an ideal commonwealth. Earlier on this ladder, Virgil's Aeneid begins with a storm and a shipwreck too.

items: Is forgiveness "rarer" and nobler than revenge? Is it always right to forgive?
What does Prospero owe Ariel and Caliban? Who has the right to rule the island?
Why does Prospero give up his magic? What would you give up, and why?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Prospero could have taken revenge but chose to forgive. Why is forgiving sometimes harder than getting even?
  2. Miranda calls the world "brave" and "new." What would you think if you saw the world for the first time?
  3. Ariel wants to be free. Caliban wants his island back. Do they both have a fair claim?
  4. Prospero says life is like a dream. What do you think he means?

Besides plays, Shakespeare wrote 154 short poems called sonnets. Every sonnet has exactly fourteen lines, and every line has a steady beat of ten syllables: da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM.

The most famous one begins by asking whether the person he loves is like a summer's day. His answer: no, you are even better, because summer ends but you will live forever in this poem. And here we are, four hundred years later, still reading it!

🧩 Try this: a couplet

Write a mini-sonnet. A real sonnet is hard, so try the last two lines, the couplet. Write two lines of about ten syllables that rhyme, about someone or something you love. ("My dog is old and slow and fond of naps, / But no one greets me better at the door." Oops, that doesn't rhyme. Try again!)

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Shake-speares Sonnets was published in 1609, probably without much help from the poet. It holds 154 sonnets and a longer poem, A Lover's Complaint. Many of the sonnets were likely written in the 1590s, when sonnet sequences were the fashion in England.

head: Sonnets
Mostly about
rows: Urging a beautiful young man to marry and have children, so his beauty will live on
Love for the young man, time, absence, jealousy, and poetry's power to last
A "dark lady" the poet loves against his own judgment
blocks.cap: The usual grouping. Who the young man and the lady were is unknown and much debated.

blocks.html: The sonnet came from Italy, where Petrarch (1300s) made it famous: eight lines, then six. English poets reshaped it into the form now named for Shakespeare: three quatrains (groups of four lines) and a closing couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, in iambic pentameter. Often the poem makes a turn (the volta) at line 9, and the couplet sums up or twists the argument.

blocks.name: gb-sonnet
blocks.cap: Switch between Sonnet 18 and Sonnet 116, and between the rhymes and the four parts.

blocks.html: The poem's boast is that verse outlasts time: the beloved will live "in eternal lines." The "lines" are both lines of verse and, perhaps, lines of descent.

blocks.title: Scanning a line
blocks.q: Mark the stresses in: "So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,"
steps: Say it aloud: so LONG as MEN can BREATHE or EYES can SEE.
Count: 10 syllables, 5 stresses, each weak syllable followed by a strong one.
That is five iambs: iambic pentameter.

blocks.html: Reading every sonnet as a true diary. The sonnets may draw on real feelings, but they are also artful performances in a fashionable form. We do not know how much is autobiography.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Time is the great villain of the sonnets: his "bending sickle" mows down beauty and youth. Against him the poet sets three defenses: children (1–17), love itself (116), and poetry (18, 55, 60, 65). Following that thread through the sequence is a good way to read it.

items: Can words really outlast time? What else lasts?
Is true love really unchanging, as Sonnet 116 says? What would change your mind?
Why might a strict form like the sonnet help a poet rather than limit him?

blocks.html: Petrarch and Dante (earlier on this ladder) wrote love poems that shaped the sonnet. Milton, later, wrote sonnets on politics and faith, proving the form could hold any subject.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Sonnet 18 says the poem will keep its subject alive forever. Has it? Who is the poem's subject?
  2. Sonnet 116 says love "alters not." Do you agree that real love does not change?
  3. Why do you think poets like strict rules, like fourteen lines and a set rhyme?
  4. If you could make one thing last forever by writing about it, what would you choose?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In a village in La Mancha, in the middle of Spain, lived a thin, gray-haired gentleman who loved to read. His favorite books were about knights: brave heroes who rode out to fight giants, rescue princesses and defeat wicked enchanters. He read so many that he began to believe every word.

One day he put on his great-grandfather's rusty armor, named his bony old horse Rocinante, chose a farm girl he had hardly met as his lady (he called her Dulcinea), named himself Don Quixote of La Mancha, and rode out to be a knight. Soon he talked a round, practical farmer named Sancho Panza into riding with him as his squire, on a donkey.
Everywhere they go, Don Quixote sees adventure. An inn becomes a castle. A flock of sheep becomes an army. And one morning, on the windy plain, he sees thirty or forty giants waving their arms...
