blocks.cap: Slide to see the plain through Sancho's eyes, or Don Quixote's.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this: draw it twice

Two pairs of eyes. Pick something ordinary in your house (the vacuum cleaner, a coat on a hook, the bathtub). Draw it twice: once as it really is, and once as Don Quixote might see it. Then write what Sancho would say to talk him out of it.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616) lived a life as full of adventure as any romance. He was wounded at the great sea battle of Lepanto (1571) and lost the use of his left hand; he was captured by pirates and held in Algiers for five years, trying four times to escape; back in Spain he worked as a tax collector and was jailed over his accounts. In his late fifties he published The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha (1605). It was a hit at once.

The book began as a parody of the romances of chivalry, long tales of knights such as Amadis of Gaul, which were wildly popular in Spain. In Chapter VI the village priest and barber hold a comic trial of Don Quixote's library and burn most of it, sparing the books they think good. But the story grew into something much larger: a long conversation between a dreamer and a realist, and a portrait of all of Spain on the road.

Don Quixote charges anyway. A sail catches his lance and sends horse and rider tumbling. His explanation: an enchanter must have turned the giants into windmills to rob him of the glory. That pattern, a vision, a collision with reality, and a new story to save the vision, repeats through the book.

blocks.html: Sancho Panza joins for the promise of an island to govern. He is earthy, fond of food and sleep, full of proverbs, and often wiser than his master about the world; Don Quixote is learned, brave, courteous, and wrong about almost everything he sees. Over the book each rubs off on the other: Sancho starts to dream, and Don Quixote starts to doubt. Their talk on the road is the heart of the novel.

Part One is also a collection: shepherds' love stories, a tale read aloud at an inn ("The Ill-Advised Curiosity"), and the story of a captive escaped from Algiers that echoes Cervantes's own. In Chapter IX the narrator claims he found the rest of the history in Arabic notebooks by one Cide Hamete Benengeli, a joke about storytellers that grows in Part Two.

Many critics call Don Quixote the first modern novel: a long prose story about ordinary life, told with irony, in which characters change. It was translated into English by Thomas Shelton as early as 1612; John Ormsby's translation (1885) is the one quoted here. The words quixotic (nobly but impractically idealistic) and "tilting at windmills" come from it.

Thinking Don Quixote is only a joke at the knight's expense. Cervantes laughs at him, but also lets him be generous, brave and right about some things that matter: honor, kindness, the dignity of a promise. Readers have argued ever since whether he is a fool, a hero or both.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Don Quixote goes mad from reading, and lives as if life were a book. Every reader of this ladder might ask: how do the books we read shape what we see? In Dante's Inferno, earlier, two lovers say a book about Lancelot led them astray (Canto V); Flaubert's Madame Bovary, later in literature, is another reader undone by romances.

items: Is it better to see the world as it is, like Sancho, or as it ought to be, like Don Quixote?
Is Don Quixote mad, or the only person who takes ideals seriously?
Why does a story about a failed knight still move readers four hundred years later?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Have you ever imagined something so hard that you almost believed it? What happened?
  2. Would you rather travel with Don Quixote or with Sancho? Why?
  3. Don Quixote wants to help people, but often makes things worse. Do good intentions matter if the results are bad?
  4. Why do you think people today call a hopeless but noble cause "tilting at windmills"?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Ten years after the first book, Cervantes wrote a second part. Now something funny has happened: Don Quixote and Sancho are famous. People they meet have read the first book about them! Some laugh at them, some admire them, and a rich Duke and Duchess play tricks on them for fun.

The Duke even makes Sancho governor of an "island" (really a little town). Everyone expects the simple farmer to make a fool of himself. Instead, he solves hard cases so wisely that people are amazed. After ten days, he decides he would rather be free and goes back to his donkey.

blocks.text: A book that knows it is a book

blocks.html: Part Two appeared in 1615, a year before Cervantes died. In its third chapter a student, Sansón Carrasco, tells the knight and squire that the history of their adventures has been printed and read by thousands. From then on, people they meet know them from Part One, and Don Quixote must live up to, and argue with, his own book.

blocks.html: In 1614, while Cervantes was writing, another author under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda published a false "second part." Cervantes struck back inside the novel: his characters meet a man from the false book, and Don Quixote changes his route from Zaragoza to Barcelona to prove the other book wrong.

The longest episode takes place at the castle of a Duke and Duchess who have read Part One and stage elaborate pranks to make the pair act out their roles. Many readers find these chapters the cruelest in the book: the noble hosts, not the madman, look foolish and unkind.

As a prank, the Duke makes Sancho governor of the "island" of Barataria. Before he leaves, Don Quixote gives him advice on governing: be humble, know yourself, judge with mercy and with care. Sancho, who cannot read, then judges cases with surprising wisdom, for instance finding money hidden in a walking stick, and chooses mercy in a famous puzzle about a bridge and an oath. After ten days of being starved by a doctor and attacked in a staged invasion, he resigns, saying he prefers the freedom of his old life.
In Barcelona, Sansón Carrasco, disguised as the Knight of the White Moon, defeats Don Quixote and makes him promise to go home for a year. At home he falls ill, sleeps, and wakes in his right mind.

Sancho, the realist, now begs his master to ride out again as a shepherd: the squire has caught the dream. The book closes with Cide Hamete's pen, hung up for good, declaring that Don Quixote was born for him alone, "and I for him."

Reading the ending as a simple happy one. Don Quixote's return to sanity is also a kind of loss, and readers have long felt torn: is it wiser to live without illusions, or does something noble die with them?

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Part Two plays with who is telling the story, who is reading it, and what is "true" in a book. Writers of the last two centuries, from novelists to philosophers, have seen it as the first great novel about the novel itself.

items: What changes when people know your story before they know you?
Is Sancho a good governor because he is simple, or because he has learned from his master?
Is it better to die sane, like Alonso Quixano, or to live with a noble dream?
Who is the real fool in the Duke's castle?

blocks.html: Shakespeare died the same spring as Cervantes, in 1616. Both created characters, Falstaff and Sancho, Hamlet and the knight, who seem to step off the page. Later on this ladder, Fielding, Dickens and Dostoevsky (who called Don Quixote the saddest book ever written) all learned from Cervantes.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. If you found a book about yourself, what would you hope it said?
  2. Sancho turned out to be a good governor. What makes someone a good leader?
  3. Was it kind or unkind for the Duke and Duchess to play tricks on Don Quixote? Why?
  4. At the end, Sancho wants his master to keep dreaming. Who changed more over the two books, the knight or the squire?
